newsitem.title: CHINA: China calls for tougher crime crackdown in 1997.
newsitem.headline: China calls for tougher crime crackdown in 1997.

text.p: China's top judge has urged police to intensify their "Strike Hard" battle against crime next year, citing the need to eradicate social instability, the Procuratorial Daily said on Wednesday.

Social stability was essential in a year that would see the return of the British territory of Hong Kong to Chinese rule as well as the convening of the Communist Party's five-yearly congress, President of the Supreme People's Court Ren Jianxin was quoted as saying.
"All factors that can possibly result in instability must be absolutely ruled out," the newspaper quoted Ren as telling a conference in Beijing on Tuesday to discuss political affairs and law.

Fears of social instability have become a major factor in decision-making by China's leaders since the 1989 student demonstrations for democracy that were crushed by the army and with the deterioration in the health of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, now 92.
The intensification in 1997 of the Strike Hard crackdown would focus on crimes ranging from murder, armed robbery and drugs offences to theft and underworld crimes, he said.
The Strike Hard campaign launched last April was China's biggest nationwide crackdown and had resulted in a major impact in maintaining social order, Ren said.

In the first three months of the campaign, more than 160,000 people were arrested and at least 1,000, and possibly many more, were executed. Executions in China are carried out almost immediately after sentencing.

Violent crime and corruption, virtually eliminated in the years after the communists swept to power in 1949, have staged a swift comeback in recent years, springing up along with economic reforms that have loosened central controls while increasing opportunities for abuse of power.

Execution and heavy prison terms have failed to curb the rising tide of crime and the Strike Hard campaign was launched partly in response to popular dissatisfaction with the government's resolve to tackle crime.
Ren also called for harsher penalties for financial and white-collar crime, saying the imposition of a fine instead of a criminal penalty should be forbidden.
Control of China's huge migrant, or floating, population that is estimated at more than 80 million, should be tightened, he said.

Many rural labourers have left the land in search of work in the cities, providing manpower for factories and construction crews. However, the mass migration has triggered new social problems and rising crime when jobs are unavailable.
